title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve

Review
What’s a z-score again?


Z-Score

How many standard deviations a single score (an \(x\)) sits above or below the mean.

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Z-scores
Why do we care?
Z-scores re-express the original data points (the \(x\)’s) so we can see, at a glance:

How close that \(x\) is to the mean
Where it falls in the spread of the distribution
How similar this participant is to the rest of the sample
How different this participant is from the majority of the sample

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Z-scores
Who’s more than 2 SD below the mean?

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Z-scores
Going backwards: Imagine that \(\color{orange}{s} = 2\) and \(\color{blue}{\bar{x}} = 25\)






Formula


\[x = \color{blue}{\bar{x}} + z\,\color{orange}{s}\]




\(z = 1 \Rightarrow x = 25 + (1)(2) = 27\)
\(z = -2 \Rightarrow x = 25 + (-2)(2) = 21\)
\(z = 0.5 \Rightarrow x = 25 + (0.5)(2) = 26\)

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Calculating a Z-score
Step-by-Step






Two steps



Mean-center the \(x\) values: \(x - \color{blue}{\bar{x}}\) — this makes the mean \(= 0\).
Divide by the standard deviation: \(\dfrac{x - \color{blue}{\bar{x}}}{\color{orange}{s}}\) — this makes the SD \(= 1\).

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Calculating Probability
Use the normal distribution

The average grade on the exam was an 86 with a standard deviation of 4.

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Calculating Probability
What is the probability of scoring a 94 or higher?

The average grade on the exam was an 86 with a standard deviation of 4.

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Calculating Probability
What is the probability of scoring a 94 or higher?






Solution



\(z = \dfrac{x-\color{blue}{\bar{x}}}{\color{orange}{s}} = \dfrac{94-86}{4} = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2\)
Beyond \(z = 2\) is the 2.1% + 0.1% slivers of the curve ≈ 2.3% chance.

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Example 2
Test Time!

The mean exam score was 86 with a standard deviation of 4. What is the probability of scoring between an 82 and a 90?

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Example 2
Test Time!

The mean exam score was 86 with a standard deviation of 4. What is the probability of scoring between an 82 and a 90?

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Example 2
Test Time!






Solution



\(z = \dfrac{82-86}{4} = \dfrac{-4}{4} = -1\)
\(z = \dfrac{90-86}{4} = \dfrac{4}{4} = 1\)
Between \(z = -1\) and \(z = 1\): a 68.3% chance of scoring between 82 and 90.

text:
Example 3
Esmeralda’s Second Test: \(\color{blue}{\bar{x}} = 72 \mid \color{orange}{s} = 6\)






Solution



\(z = \dfrac{60-72}{6} = \dfrac{-12}{6} = -2\)
About a 2.3% chance that she failed.
What’s the chance she passed?
\(100\% - 2.3\% = 97.7\%\)

Because the standard normal curve is standard and normal, we can look up the exact probability for a z-score with decimals.

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Z-scores and Probability
The Z-Table






Rule


The z-table gives you the probability of that z-score or less (the area to the left).




If you need that z-score or higher, subtract the table value from 1.

Esmeralda: .023 chance of failing, so a 1 - .023 = .977 → 97.7% chance of passing.

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Z-scores and Probability
Life Satisfaction

In a recent study on world happiness, participants were asked to evaluate their current lives on a scale from 0 to 10, where 0 represents the worst possible life and 10 represents the best possible life. The responses were normally distributed, with a mean of 5.4 and a standard deviation of 2.2. Find the probability that a randomly selected study participant’s response was:



Less than 4
More than 8

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Z-scores and Probability
Life Satisfaction: \(\color{blue}{\bar{x}} = 5.4 \mid \color{orange}{s} = 2.2\)






Convert to z first



Less than 4: \(z = \dfrac{4-5.4}{2.2} = \dfrac{-1.4}{2.2} = -0.64\)
More than 8: \(z = \dfrac{8-5.4}{2.2} = \dfrac{2.6}{2.2} = 1.18\)

MENSA

Scores on an IQ test are approximately normal with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. The organization MENSA, which calls itself the “high IQ society,” requires a score of 130 or higher.

\(z = \dfrac{x-\color{blue}{\bar{x}}}{\color{orange}{s}} = \dfrac{130-100}{15} = \dfrac{30}{15} = 2\)

text:
Z-table clarity
The table only ever looks left









Hover over the curve. Shaded = the table value. Left of z: read it directly. Right of z: 1 minus the table value. Between: big area minus small area. The “1 minus” applies to the area, never to \(z\).

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Z-scores
“Compared to what?” is everywhere



Newborn weight


Is a 4.3 kg baby big? (\(\mu = 3.4\), \(\sigma = 0.5\))


Raw (kg)z-score






















\(z = \dfrac{4.3-3.4}{0.5} = 1.8\). Growth charts report exactly this.






Daily screen time


Is 7 hours a lot? (\(\mu = 4.5\), \(\sigma = 1.5\))


Raw (hours)z-score






















\(z = \dfrac{7-4.5}{1.5} = 1.67\)






Bolt diameter


Is 10.10 mm out of spec? (\(\mu = 10.00\), \(\sigma = 0.05\))


Raw (mm)z-score






















\(z = \dfrac{10.10-10.00}{0.05} = 2.0\). Quality control flags this.






One-day stock return


Is a \(-2.15\%\) day unusual? (\(\mu = 0.05\%\), \(\sigma = 1.1\%\))


Raw (%)z-score






















\(z = \dfrac{-2.15-0.05}{1.1} = -2.0\)

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
Learning Goals

Compute sample mean and standard deviation by hand.
Interpret what the mean and SD tell us about data.
Standardize raw scores into Z-scores.
Interpret Z-scores (direction and distance from mean).
Relate Z-scores to probability under a normal curve.

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
1. Mean Calculation
Sample Mean Calculation

A psychology researcher collects the following data on the number of hours five participants spent practicing a task: 3, 5, 8, 2, 7.

Question: What is the average number of hours spent practicing?




Manual Solution


\(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum(3+5+8+2+7)}{5} = \frac{25}{5} = 5\text{ hours}\)





Code Solution


mean(c(3,5,8,2,7))

[1] 5

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
2. Mean Calculation
Sample Mean Calculation

A study measures the changes in mood scores before and after an intervention. The changes in mood scores are: -4, -2, 0, 3, 5.

Question: Calculate the mean change in mood score.




Manual Solution


\(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum(-4 + (-2) + 0 + 3 + 5)}{5} = \frac{2}{5} = 0.4\)





Code Solution


mean(c(-4,-2,0,3,5))

[1] 0.4

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
3. Standard Deviation Calculation
Sample Standard Deviation

A psychologist measures the number of stressful events experienced by a small group of participants over a week: 2, 3, 6, 4, 5.

Question: Calculate the standard deviation of stressful events.


Manual Solution




First compute the sample mean: \(\bar{x} = \frac{2+3+6+4+5}{5} = \frac{20}{5} = 4.\)


Compute squared deviations: \((2-4)^2=4,\ (3-4)^2=1,\ (6-4)^2=4,\ (4-4)^2=0,\ (5-4)^2=1\)


Sum of squares = \(4+1+4+0+1 = 10\)


Sample variance \(s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})^2}{n-1} = \frac{10}{4} = 2.5\)


Sample SD \(s = \sqrt{2.5} \approx 1.58\)






Code Solution


sd(c(2,3,6,4,5))

[1] 1.581139

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
4. Standard Deviation Calculation
Sample Standard Deviation

Sample Standard Deviation Participants’ anxiety scores in a clinical trial are recorded as: 4, 7, 3, 5, 8, 6, 2.

Question: Compute the standard deviation of these anxiety scores.




Solution


First compute the sample mean: \(\bar{x} = \frac{4+7+3+5+8+6+2}{7} = \frac{35}{7} = 5\) Squared deviations: \((4-5)^2=1\\(7-5)^2=4\\ (3-5)^2=4\\(5-5)^2=0\\(8-5)^2=9\\(6-5)^2=1\\ (2-5)^2=9\\\)  Sum = \(1+4+4+0+9+1+9 = 28\). \(s^2 = \frac{28}{7-1} = 4.67\), so \(s = \sqrt{4.67} \approx 2.16\).





Code Solution


sd(c(4,7,3,5,8,6,2))

[1] 2.160247

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
5. Standard Deviation Calculation
Interpreting Standard Deviation in Psychology

A researcher finds that the standard deviation of reaction times in a cognitive task is 1.5 seconds. Another researcher finds a standard deviation of 0.5 seconds for a similar task.

Question: Which task shows more variability in participants’ reaction times, and what might this indicate about task difficulty?


Solution


A standard deviation of 1.5 is is larger than 0.5 is, so the first task shows more variability.

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
6. Z-Score Calculation
Z-Score for a Single Value

In a personality study, the average score on an extraversion scale is 50, with a standard deviation of 10. One participant scores 70.

Question: What is the Z-score for this participant?




Solution


\(z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{70 - 50}{10} = \frac{20}{10} = 2\)





Code Solution


(70-50)/10

[1] 2

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
7. Z-Score Calculation:
Interpreting Z-Scores

A participant in a self-esteem survey has a Z-score of -1.5. The mean self-esteem score for the survey is 40, and the standard deviation is 5.

Question: Did this participant score above or below the mean, and by how many standard deviations?


Solution


A Z-score of -1.5 is below the mean. In raw score terms: \(X = \mu + z\sigma = 40 + (-1.5)(5) = 40 - 7.5 = 32.5.\) So the participant scored 32.5, which is 1.5 standard deviations below the mean.

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
8. Z-Score Calculation
Z-Score with Negative Value

The mean stress score of a group is 25, with a standard deviation of 4. If a participant has a stress score of 18…

Question: Calculate their Z-score and interpret its meaning in the context of stress levels.




Solution


\(z = \frac{18 - 25}{4} = \frac{-7}{4} = -1.75.\) The Z-score is \(z \approx -1.75\), meaning this participant’s stress score is 1.75 standard deviations below the group mean — they have substantially lower stress than average.





Code Solution


(18-25)/4

[1] -1.75

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
9. Z-Score Calculation
Multiple Z-Scores

In a clinical assessment, the average depression score is 60, with a standard deviation of 8. Two participants have scores of 72 and 48.

Question: Calculate the Z-scores for both participants and explain what the values tell us about their relative positions in the group.


Solution




For the first participant (72): \(z_1 = \frac{72 - 60}{8} = \frac{12}{8} = 1.5.\)


For the second participant (48): \(z_2 = \frac{48 - 60}{8} = \frac{-12}{8} = -1.5.\)


Interpretation: the first participant is 1.5 SD above the mean (higher depression score than average), while the second is 1.5 SD below the mean (lower depression score than average). They are symmetric around the mean.






Code Solution


(72-60)/8;(48-60)/8

[1] 1.5


[1] -1.5

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
10. Z-Scores to Raw Scores
Working Backwards

The distribution of scores on a math test is approximately normal with mean \(\mu = 100\) and standard deviation \(\sigma = 15\).

Question: What raw score corresponds to \(z = 1.2\)?




Solution


Solve \(z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\) for \(x\): \(x = \mu + z\sigma = 100 + 1.2(15) = 118\)





Code Solution


1.2*15 + 100

[1] 118

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
Reading the Z-Table






The table only ever gives the area to the left of z



Sketch the curve and shade what the question asks for.
Left of z: read the table value directly.
Right of z: 1 minus the table value (subtract the area, not \(z\)).
Between two z’s: big area minus small area.




Anxiety scores are approximately normal with \(\mu = 50\) and \(\sigma = 10\).

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
11. Probability: Left Tail
Below a Score
Question: What proportion of people score below 42?




Solution



\(z = \frac{42-50}{10} = -0.80\)


Shade the left tail. The table gives the left area directly: \(.2119\)


About 21.2% score below 42.






Code Solution


pnorm(-0.80)                       # z-table

[1] 0.2118554

pnorm(42, mean = 50, sd = 10)      # unrounded z

[1] 0.2118554

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
12. Probability: Right Tail
Above a Score
Question: What proportion of people score above 65?




Solution



\(z = \frac{65-50}{10} = 1.50\)


Shade the right tail. The table gives the area to the left (\(.9332\)), so subtract from 1: \(1 - .9332 = .0668\)


About 6.7% score above 65.






Code Solution


1 - pnorm(1.50)                                       # z-table

[1] 0.0668072

pnorm(65, mean = 50, sd = 10, lower.tail = FALSE)     # unrounded z

[1] 0.0668072

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
13. Probability: Between Two Scores
Between Two Values
Question: What proportion of people score between 45 and 60?




Solution



\(z_{45} = \frac{45-50}{10} = -0.50\) and \(z_{60} = \frac{60-50}{10} = 1.00\)


Table: left of \(1.00\) is \(.8413\); left of \(-0.50\) is \(.3085\)


Big area minus small area: \(.8413 - .3085 = .5328\)


About 53.3% score between 45 and 60.






Code Solution


pnorm(1.00) - pnorm(-0.50)                            # z-table

[1] 0.5328072

pnorm(60, 50, 10) - pnorm(45, 50, 10)                 # unrounded z

[1] 0.5328072

Sample Means

Once each of you collects 500 responses, you calculate the average answer, the mean of your sample.



\(\bar{x}_1 = \dfrac{x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + \cdots + x_{500}}{500}\)
One mean per sample: \(\bar{x}_1, \bar{x}_2, \ldots, \bar{x}_{30}\).

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Sampling Theory
The big idea

Sampling theory is the body of principles that tells us how statistics from samples behave, so that we can make inferences about the population the samples came from.


Take every possible sample of size \(n\) from a population and compute the mean of each. Those means form the sampling distribution of the mean.
It is conceptual and theoretical. We never actually collect every possible sample.

What it buys us

The sampling distribution of the mean is centered on \(\mu\), has standard deviation \(SE = \sigma / \sqrt{n}\), and is approximately normal for large \(n\).
That lets us find the probability of getting a particular sample mean.
We will use that probability to gauge significance in our inferential statistics.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Standard Error
The Standard Error of the Mean

\(SE = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

\(\sigma\) = Population Standard Deviation
\(n\) - Sample Size

The Standard Error is not just another name for \(\sigma\) — it’s the standard deviation of the distribution of sample means, which is why it shrinks as \(n\) grows (\(SE = \sigma / \sqrt{n}\)).
In other words: \(\sigma\) describes how spread out individual scores are; \(SE\) describes how spread out sample means are.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
The Lady Tasting Tea
The story

A lady declares that by tasting a cup of tea made with milk she can discriminate whether the milk or the tea infusion was first added to the cup. We will consider the problem of designing an experiment by means of which this assertion can be tested. […] [It] consists in mixing eight cups of tea, four in one way and four in the other, and presenting them to the subject for judgment in a random order. The subject has been told in advance of that the test will consist, namely, that she will be asked to taste eight cups, that these shall be four of each kind […]. — Fisher, 1935.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
The Lady Tasting Tea
The design

A lady claimed she could tell whether milk or tea was poured first.
Fisher designed an experiment:

8 cups of tea
4 poured milk-first, 4 tea-first
Randomized order

The lady must classify each cup.




A classic example of hypothesis testing, based on R.A. Fisher’s 1935 design.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
The Hypotheses
Lady tasting tea






Null hypothesis \(H_0\)


The lady has no special ability; she is just guessing.









Alternative hypothesis \(H_1/H_A\)


The lady can tell the difference.




Key idea: we begin by assuming \(H_0\) is true.
We only reject \(H_0\) if the data are too surprising under \(H_0\).

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Possible Outcomes
How many cups does she classify correctly?
For 8 cups (4 of each), under \(H_0\) the number correct can only be 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8.










Correct
Probability




8
1 / 70 ≈ 1.4%


6
16 / 70 ≈ 22.9%


4
36 / 70 ≈ 51.4%


2
16 / 70 ≈ 22.9%


0
1 / 70 ≈ 1.4%

title: Sampling Theory
text:
The Test
Fisher’s rule

Reject \(H_0\) only if she gets all 8 correct.
Under \(H_0\) there are \({8 \choose 4} = \dfrac{8!}{4!\,(8-4)!} = 70\) equally likely ways to guess which 4 cups are milk-first.
So the probability of guessing all 8 correctly by chance is \(\dfrac{1}{70} \approx 1.4\%\).

Since \(1.4\%\) is less than \(5\%\), it is rare enough to count as evidence against \(H_0\).

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Decision & Interpretation
Lady tasting tea








8 of 8 correct: reject \(H_0\)


If she were just guessing, a result this extreme happens about 1.4% of the time. That is evidence she can tell the difference.










6 of 8 correct: fail to reject \(H_0\)


If she were just guessing, getting 6 or more right happens about \(\frac{1 + 16}{70} = 24.3\%\) of the time. That is not unusual enough.





We never prove the alternative; we only judge whether the data are too unlikely under the null.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
The Logic
Same logic for t-tests, z-tests, and many modern methods

Assume a null model.
Compute how likely the observed data (or more extreme data) are under that model. That probability is the p-value.
If the p-value is very small (below \(\alpha\), typically .05), reject the null.

# Correct cups out of 8 = 2k, so all 8 correct means k = 4

Example: Millennials and Gen Z

Professor Brocker wants to know if Millennials enjoy the Netflix Original Dark more than Gen Z does. He recruits 500 Millennials and 500 Gen Z students and asks them to rate Dark on a scale of 1 to 10 (10 being fantastic). Participants are not randomly assigned to generation, so this is a quasi-experiment.


Hypothesis: Millennials will rate their enjoyment of Dark higher than their Gen Z peers.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Hypothesis
Example: Millennials and Gen Z

Null hypothesis: the mean rating is the same for both generations.

\(H_0: \mu_{\text{Millennial}} = \mu_{\text{Gen Z}}\)

Alternative hypothesis: the mean rating is higher for Millennials.

\(H_A: \mu_{\text{Millennial}} > \mu_{\text{Gen Z}}\)





Some texts write the null for a directional test as \(\mu_{\text{Millennial}} \leq \mu_{\text{Gen Z}}\). The decision rule is the same.

Alternative Hypothesis: Millennials will rate their enjoyment of Dark as significantly higher than their Gen Z peers.
Null Hypothesis: Millennials and Gen Z will not differ in their rating of enjoyment of the Dark.

Example 1

Professor Brocker wants to know if giving his students coffee will improve their exam scores. He randomly assigns 13 of his 26 students to drink a doubleshot; he calls this the experimental group. The other 13 students drink decaf (a placebo); he calls this the control group.


\(H_0\): \(\mu_\text{Coffee} = \mu_\text{Decaf}\)
\(H_1/H_A\): \(\mu_\text{Coffee} > \mu_\text{Decaf}\)

Esmeralda gives an anti-depressant to 100 individuals suffering from depression. She gives another 100 individuals a placebo. After 2 months, we measure their depression.


\(H_0\): \(\mu_\text{SSRI} = \mu_\text{Placebo}\)
\(H_1/H_A\): \(\mu_\text{SSRI} < \mu_\text{Placebo}\)

In science, we do not say that we proved anything.

Nothing is ever really proven.

title: Sampling Theory
text:

In science, we do not say that we have proven anything.
Our findings will be stated in terms of the Null Hypothesis.

Failing is ‘bad’

One student’s sample of \(n = 500\) has \(M = 6.75\). If \(\mu = 6.6\) and \(\sigma = 1.5\), how unusual is a sample mean this high?

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Decisions
Reject or fail to reject \(H_0\)

In science, we do not say that we proved anything. Our decision is stated in terms of the null hypothesis \(H_0\).
The decision depends on the p-value: the probability of getting data at least this extreme if \(H_0\) were true.









Reject \(H_0\) (\(p \leq \alpha\))


The data would be unlikely if \(H_0\) were true. The data are consistent with \(H_A\), but that is not a proof of \(H_A\).










Fail to reject \(H_0\) (\(p > \alpha\))


The data are not unlikely enough under \(H_0\). This is not evidence that \(H_0\) is true. A small sample or a noisy measure can hide a real effect.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
Decisions
Neither outcome is a verdict on the study

Rejecting \(H_0\) is the result we usually hope to see, but a well-run study that fails to reject is still informative.
Failing to reject means “we did not find convincing evidence of a difference,” not “there is no difference.”
When reporting a result, state the decision about \(H_0\) and give the test statistic and p-value.
